whyNot: The **suprachiasmatic nucleus** is the circadian clock receiving light input that drives orexin release; it does not make histamine.
The **locus coeruleus** supplies norepinephrine and richly expresses OX1 receptors; it is not where histamine is made.
The **raphe nuclei** release serotonin onto the basal forebrain and thalamus, not histamine.
The **VLPO** is the GABA sleep center that histamine inhibits, not the source of histamine neurons.
q10-01.why: In the brain histamine is made solely by cells of the **tuberomammillary nucleus** of the hypothalamus, a small bilateral nucleus that sends histaminergic fibers to nearly all brain regions and the spinal cord.

whyNot: There is no apparent histamine **reuptake** pump, so released histamine simply diffuses widely away from its synapse.
**COMT** is not part of the histamine pathway the book describes, which is methylation followed by MAO-B.
**Acetylcholinesterase** is not among the enzymes the book names for histamine, which are HNMT and then MAO-B.
**Diamine oxidase** clears histamine only outside the brain; the brain uses a two-enzyme sequence.
q10-02.why: Brain histamine is cleared by two enzymes in sequence: **HNMT** makes N-methylhistamine, then **MAO-B** converts it to an inactive product; with no reuptake pump, histamine diffuses away widely.

whyNot: Blocking **H1** removes histamine's alerting signal and causes sedation, the opposite of promoting wakefulness.
The **polyamine site** is an allosteric spot on NMDA receptors where histamine can act, not a receptor that gates histamine release.
**H2** receptors are postsynaptic, signal through cAMP, and do not appear directly linked to wakefulness.
**H4** receptors have not been found in the brain, so they cannot control central histamine release.
q10-03.why: **H3** receptors are presynaptic autoreceptors that act as a gate on histamine release; blocking them (as pitolisant does) opens the gate, releases histamine and promotes wakefulness.

whyNot: **Adenosine** is the homeostatic sleep-drive signal that builds with time awake, not the effector of histamine's alerting action.
**Chloride channels** are not part of H1 signaling, which runs through a G-protein second-messenger system.
**GIRK** inactivation is an orexin 2 receptor effect, not the H1 pathway.
**cAMP and CREB** are the H2 pathway, which has no direct tie to wakefulness.
q10-04.why: Postsynaptic **H1** receptors couple to a G-protein pathway that activates phosphatidylinositol and the transcription factor **cFOS**, producing wakefulness and alertness; H2 uses cAMP/PKA/CREB instead.

whyNot: **Hypocretin** is only the alternate name for the same peptides (orexin A and B); it is not a separate OX2-selective peptide.
Orexin A, not orexin B, reaches **OX1**; orexin B does not bind OX1 at all.
**Orexin A** interacts with both OX1 and OX2, so it is not the OX2-selective peptide.
One of the two peptides, **orexin B**, is selective for OX2.
q10-05.why: The two orexin peptides differ in reach: orexin A can act on both OX1 and OX2, whereas **orexin B** binds selectively to OX2.

whyNot: **VLPO GABA neurons** form the sleep-promoting center that wakefulness suppresses; orexin's wake action is not exerted through them.
**Cerebellar Purkinje cells** are not part of the orexin wake circuit; OX2 is highlighted in the histaminergic TMN.
The **pineal** gland secretes melatonin and is not the OX2-rich site that carries orexin's wake effect.
**Spinal motor neurons** are not named as orexin's wake target; the book ties OX2 to the histaminergic TMN.
q10-06.why: Orexin's wake-stabilizing effect runs largely through **OX2 receptors** that are densely expressed on the histaminergic neurons of the **TMN**, which then release histamine across the brain.

whyNot: The **thalamus** receives orexin projections; it does not contain the orexin neurons themselves.
Orexin cell bodies are found only in hypothalamic areas, so a midbrain site like the **substantia nigra** is wrong.
The **basal forebrain** receives orexin input and releases acetylcholine but does not house orexin neurons.
The **locus coeruleus** is a target that releases norepinephrine and expresses OX1, not the origin of orexin neurons.
q10-07.why: Orexin/hypocretin neurons are found **only in hypothalamic areas** (lateral, perifornical and posterior) and project widely; these are the neurons that degenerate in narcolepsy.

whyNot: **Histamine** is an arousal transmitter released from the TMN that promotes waking, not the substance that builds up as sleep pressure.
**Orexin** belongs to the opposing circadian wake drive via the SCN, not the homeostatic sleep drive.
**Melatonin** is secreted at night in the dark and relates to circadian timing, not to the buildup that tracks time awake.
**Cortisol** is not named in the sleep-drive mechanism; the book ties homeostatic drive to adenosine.
q10-08.why: Homeostatic sleep drive tracks time awake because **adenosine** accumulates, then disinhibits the VLPO so that GABA is released to inhibit the wake-promoting centers.

whyNot: **Histamine** is a wake-promoting transmitter from the TMN, which the VLPO suppresses rather than uses.
**Orexin** stabilizes wakefulness from the lateral hypothalamus; it is the signal whose fall lets the VLPO take over.
The book names **GABA**, not glutamate, as the transmitter of the sleep-promoting VLPO.
**Acetylcholine** is an arousal transmitter from the basal forebrain and PPT/LDT that the VLPO suppresses.
q10-09.why: The sleep-promoting **VLPO** releases **GABA** onto the TMN and the other arousal centers, inhibiting histamine, norepinephrine, serotonin, dopamine and acetylcholine so sleep can take over.

whyNot: **Stage 1** is not the acetylcholine peak; the book places that peak in REM sleep.
**Stage 2** is where dopamine, norepinephrine, serotonin and histamine peak, whereas acetylcholine peaks in REM.
Acetylcholine is not **constant**; it swings between a stage 4 low and a REM high each cycle.
**Stage 4** is the acetylcholine low point, the opposite of its peak.
q10-10.why: Acetylcholine tracks the stage 4 to REM swing of each sleep cycle, bottoming in stage 4 and **peaking in REM**, when cortical activity resembles wakefulness.

whyNot: **Wakefulness** is when these arousal circuits are active; the book's trough for these transmitters is REM, with a peak in stage 2 sleep.
**Stage 3** is deeper slow-wave sleep, not the trough; the lowest levels are in REM.
**Stage 1** is not singled out; these transmitters fall lowest only in REM and peak in stage 2.
**Stage 2** is the peak, not the trough, for dopamine, norepinephrine, serotonin and histamine.
q10-11.why: Dopamine, norepinephrine, serotonin and histamine rise to a peak in stage 2 sleep and drop to their **lowest in REM**, the stage in which acetylcholine is highest.

whyNot: The book links **growth hormone** release to slow-wave sleep, which GHB deepens; sleep loss is not described as raising it.
**Opposite direction:** disturbed sleep lowers appetite-inhibiting leptin rather than raising it, and raises ghrelin.
**Melatonin** is secreted at night in the dark with normal sleep; insomnia biology shows reduced nocturnal secretion.
**Cortisol** is not the change named for impaired sleep; related insomnia biology shows HPA-axis activation, an increase.
q10-12.why: Disturbed sleep lowers the appetite-inhibiting hormone **leptin** and raises the appetite-stimulating hormone **ghrelin**, along with gut dysbiosis, which raises the odds of obesity, diabetes and heart disease.

whyNot: Insomnia biology shows **reduced** nocturnal melatonin secretion, not an excess.
Loss of **orexin neurons** is the narcolepsy pathology; in insomnia, excess orexin is considered as a possible driver.
That is the older view; the newest imaging evidence points away from a failure to **switch on** sleep circuits.
**Adenosine** is the sleep-drive signal; the book attributes insomnia to persistent arousal rather than low sleep pressure.
q10-13.why: Insomnia is conceptualized as nighttime **hyperarousal**: the newest imaging evidence suggests the brain cannot turn **off** its arousal circuits, rather than failing to turn on the VLPO sleep circuits.

whyNot: The suggested latency criterion is longer than **30** minutes, not 10.
**SOREMPs** are a narcolepsy marker on sleep testing, not an insomnia criterion.
The **Epworth** scale subjectively rates daytime sleepiness for hypersomnia evaluation, not insomnia.
The suggested threshold for total sleep time is under **6.5** hours, not 8.
q10-14.why: Suggested insomnia criteria quantify poor sleep: latency or wake after sleep onset over 30 minutes, total sleep under 6.5 hours, and **sleep efficiency below 85%**.

whyNot: Sevenfold is the figure for **substance use disorders**, not depression.
**1.2** does not appear in the insomnia risk figure, whose depression value is far higher.
Twofold is the risk for **anxiety**, not depression.
**Ten** times does not appear; the highest risk shown is sevenfold, for substance use disorders.
q10-15.why: Insomnia is a risk factor for, or prodrome of, later psychiatric illness: about **fourfold** risk of depression, twofold for anxiety and sevenfold for substance use disorders.

whyNot: **Eszopiclone** lacks α1 selectivity and binds several α subunits, like the benzodiazepines.
**Zopiclone and eszopiclone** bind α1, α2, α3 and α5, so they are not α1-selective.
Not **all** Z drugs are selective; the zopiclone family is not.
**Zaleplon and zolpidem** do bind selectively to α1 subunits, so the answer is not none.
**Anxiolysis** is linked to the α2 and α3 subtypes, not α1.
**Alcohol potentiation** is linked to the α2 and α3 subtypes.
**Muscle relaxation** is linked to the α2 and α3 subtypes.
**Cognition** and related functions are tied to the α5 subtype, mostly in the hippocampus.
q10-17.why: The **α1** subtype is critical for sedation, so every effective GABA-A PAM hypnotic targets it; it is also linked to amnesia and anticonvulsant action, and its adaptation with chronic use is thought to cause tolerance.

whyNot: They remain **effective**; when first-line hypnotics fail, benzodiazepines still have a place in treatment.
**Liver toxicity** is not the book's reason; its concerns are tolerance, withdrawal and rebound.
**Weight gain** is raised in the book for antihistamines, not as the reason benzodiazepine hypnotics are second-line.
**Cardiac toxicity** is not given as a reason; the issues named are lost efficacy over time and withdrawal effects.
q10-18.why: Long-term use brings loss of efficacy (**tolerance**) and **withdrawal**, including rebound insomnia that can be worse than the original problem, so benzodiazepines rank behind first-line hypnotics.

whyNot: **Flurazepam** is ultra-long acting, with a half-life measured in days, not hours.
**Quazepam**, like flurazepam, is ultra-long acting, lasting days.
**Estazolam** has a moderate half-life, not an ultra-short one.
**Temazepam** has a moderate half-life, placing it in the hangover-risk group.
q10-19.why: Among the five benzodiazepines approved for insomnia, **triazolam** is the one with an ultra-short half-life of about 1 to 2 hours, unlike the day-long flurazepam and quazepam.

whyNot: Blocking **adenosine** receptors is how caffeine promotes wakefulness, the opposite of sleep.
Enhancing GABA at the VLPO describes **benzodiazepines and Z drugs**; DORAs work differently.
**H1 blockade** is the antihistamine route, a separate arousal-reducing mechanism from orexin blockade.
**Melatonin receptor agonism** is how ramelteon and tasimelteon work, not DORAs.
q10-20.why: DORAs block OX1 and OX2 receptors, especially OX2, so the orexins can no longer **stabilize wakefulness** or drive release of other wake-promoting transmitters, and the patient falls asleep.

whyNot: Neither DORA is a **GABA-A PAM**; they act by blocking orexin, not by enhancing GABA.
Comparable OX1 and OX2 affinity describes **suvorexant**, not lemborexant.
Both are **reversible** inhibitors, which lets rising morning orexin reverse the blockade.
The book credits lemborexant with faster **kinetics**, not a longer-acting profile.
q10-21.why: Lemborexant binds **OX2 more strongly than OX1**, unlike suvorexant's comparable affinity, and shows faster association and dissociation at OX2, which may imply quicker morning reversal.

whyNot: Absorption is not the issue raised; the point is competition between falling drug and rising **orexin**.
DORAs block orexin receptors in the brain's wake circuits; **peripheral-only** action is not the explanation.
They are **reversible** inhibitors, which is exactly why rising orexin can displace them.
A **threshold** does exist for DORAs, at about 65% receptor blockade.
**D2 antagonism** is not part of trazodone's hypnotic action, which is blockade of serotonin, norepinephrine and histamine pathways.
**5HT1A agonism** is not the hypnotic mechanism; the book describes 5HT2A, α1 and H1 antagonism.
**NET inhibition** is not credited; α1 blockade combined with H1 and 5HT2A antagonism produces the hypnotic effect.
**SERT inhibition** appears only at higher antidepressant doses and is not what deepens slow-wave sleep.
q10-23.why: Trazodone's **5HT2A antagonism** specifically enhances slow-wave (deep) sleep, which can correlate with restorative sleep; its α1 and H1 blockade add to the hypnotic effect.

whyNot: **α1 antagonism** is part of trazodone's arousal-reducing profile; at hypnotic doses doxepin is selective for H1 instead.
**Orexin antagonists** are the DORAs such as suvorexant; doxepin is a tricyclic acting on histamine.
**M1 antagonism** is the anticholinergic action of agents like diphenhydramine; low-dose doxepin lacks it.
**SERT and NET inhibition** occurs only at antidepressant doses of 150 to 300 mg, not at 1 to 6 mg.
q10-24.why: At 1 to 6 mg, far below antidepressant doses, doxepin's very high affinity for **H1** makes it a relatively **selective H1 antagonist**, without anticholinergic or reuptake-blocking effects.

whyNot: **α2 blockade** is not described for diphenhydramine; its anticholinergic effects come from muscarinic receptors.
**H1 blockade** produces the sedating, hypnotic effect rather than the anticholinergic side effects.
**5HT3 receptors** are not described as part of diphenhydramine's action.
**H3 blockade** would release histamine and promote wakefulness, as pitolisant does.
q10-25.why: Diphenhydramine is not selective for H1; it also blocks **muscarinic M1** receptors, which causes anticholinergic effects such as dry mouth, constipation, blurred vision and memory problems.

whyNot: **25 to 30%** is the threshold for GABA-A positive allosteric modulators, not DORAs.
**10%** is not a threshold the book gives for any hypnotic class.
About **80%** is the estimated threshold for serotonin and histamine antagonists.
**95%** is not a sleep threshold in the book; the highest estimate given is about 80%.
q10-26.why: Sleep onset depends on receptor occupancy crossing a threshold, roughly 25 to 30% for GABA-A drugs, about **65% for DORAs** and about 80% for serotonin or histamine antagonists.

whyNot: Food can delay absorption, so avoiding it is advised for slow sleep onset; it does not fix morning **grogginess**.
**Opposite direction:** grogginess calls for dosing earlier in the evening, not later.
**Caffeine** at bedtime opposes the hypnotic and does nothing to bring drug levels below threshold by morning.
**Raising** the dose is the fix for sleep that does not last long enough, and would worsen morning carryover.
q10-27.why: Morning grogginess means drug levels are still near or above the sleep threshold at wake time, so **lower the dose**, give it earlier in the evening, or switch to a drug that stays above threshold for less time.

whyNot: **Too cold** describes ultra-short half-lives of 1 to 3 hours that wear off before waking; these two last longer.
Both are **benzodiazepine hypnotics** approved for insomnia.
**Way too hot** is for ultra-long half-life agents like flurazepam and quazepam that accumulate.
**Just right** is about 8 hours above threshold, shown by agents like eszopiclone, zolpidem CR and low-dose trazodone.
q10-28.why: With moderately long half-lives (15 to 30 hours), estazolam and temazepam stay above the sleep threshold past wake time, giving the **'still too hot'** hangover of sedation and memory problems.

whyNot: **Modafinil** is approved only as an adjunct to treating the airway obstruction, not as first-line therapy.
**Melatonin** acts on circadian timing and sleep onset; it does nothing for airway obstruction.
**Sodium oxybate** is used for cataplexy and sleepiness in narcolepsy, not for airway obstruction.
**Stimulants** such as amphetamine and methylphenidate are not approved for OSA and do not treat the obstruction.
q10-29.why: Because OSA is airway obstruction, first-line treatment is **continuous positive airway pressure**; wake-promoting drugs such as modafinil only serve as adjuncts for residual sleepiness.

whyNot: Diagnostic MSLT latency is **short**, 8 minutes or less, not longer than 15.
**Long sleep** of over 10 hours is a feature of idiopathic hypersomnia, not narcolepsy.
Most narcolepsy patients are **HLA DQB1-0602** positive, so normal typing is not the diagnostic finding.
**Two or more**, not fewer than two, SOREMPs are diagnostic; fewer than two fits idiopathic hypersomnia.
q10-30.why: A CSF orexin level below **110 pg/mL** is diagnostic for narcolepsy, reflecting loss of orexin neurons; two or more SOREMPs with a short MSLT latency also count when orexin is normal.

whyNot: The book does not attribute cataplexy to **H3**; H3 blockade is a treatment strategy for sleepiness.
**Adenosine** relates to sleep drive and caffeine, not to the loss of muscle tone in cataplexy.
**Melatonin** regulates circadian timing and is not linked to cataplexy.
**Histamine** promotes wakefulness; cataplexy stems from low orexin, not from too much histamine.
q10-31.why: Orexin normally keeps motor tone stable by day and permits motor inhibition at night; with orexin neurons lost, REM-type **inhibition intrudes** into wakefulness as sudden loss of muscle tone.

whyNot: **5%** understates it greatly; the book reports a large majority of patients as positive.
**Half** is too low; most patients, especially those with cataplexy, are positive.
**20%** is the rate in the general population, not in narcolepsy.
Not **every** patient carries it; the book reports a majority, not a universal, figure.
q10-32.why: HLA DQB1-0602 is a genetic marker strongly enriched in narcolepsy: about **90%** of patients, particularly those with cataplexy, carry it, compared with only 20% of the general population.

whyNot: **HLA DQB1-0602** positivity is a narcolepsy finding, present in most but not all of those patients.
CSF orexin is not typically affected in idiopathic hypersomnia; **undetectable** levels point to narcolepsy with cataplexy.
**Opposite:** idiopathic hypersomnia involves long or normal sleep that is non-refreshing.
**Cataplexy** is a narcolepsy feature tied to orexin loss, not part of idiopathic hypersomnia.
**Non-24** mainly affects blind people who cannot entrain the clock to light; it is not called the most common.
**Irregular sleep–wake** disorder is not among the circadian disorders the chapter lists, so it cannot be the most common.
**Advanced sleep phase** disorder is linked to PER2 variants and early bed and wake times, but not called the most common.
**Shift work** disorder affects a share of shift workers across the workforce, not only nurses, and is not called the most common.
q10-34.why: **Delayed sleep phase disorder** is the most common circadian rhythm disorder; sleep is normal in duration and quality but shifted late, and it is linked to CLOCK gene polymorphisms.

whyNot: **Evening light alone** is incomplete; advanced sleep phase pairs evening light with early morning melatonin.
**Noon melatonin** is not a timing the book recommends; it advises early morning melatonin for advanced phase.
**Morning light** is the delayed-phase approach and would push an already early clock earlier.
That combination of **morning light and evening melatonin** is the delayed phase, depression and shift work regimen, the reverse of this one.
q10-35.why: Advanced sleep phase disorder needs the clock shifted **later**, so give early evening bright light and early morning melatonin; delayed sleep phase gets the reverse.

whyNot: **Zolpidem** is an α1-selective GABA-A Z drug for insomnia, not a circadian agent.
**Modafinil** is a DAT-inhibiting wake promoter for narcolepsy and shift work disorder, not for clock synchronization.
**Pitolisant** is an H3 antagonist for narcolepsy sleepiness, not a melatonin agent.
**Ramelteon** is the MT1/MT2 agonist marketed for insomnia; tasimelteon carries the non-24 indication.
q10-36.why: Blind people cannot entrain the SCN clock to light, so it free-runs; the melatonin MT1/MT2 agonist **tasimelteon** synchronizes the clock, acting at MT2 to retrain the circadian rhythm.

whyNot: **5HT2C** is a serotonin receptor, where agomelatine acts as an antagonist, separate from the MT3 site.
Orexin receptors are **OX1 and OX2**, unrelated to melatonin sites.
**H3** is a presynaptic histamine autoreceptor, not a melatonin site.
It is not a **GABA-A subunit**; the book identifies the MT3 site as an enzyme.
q10-37.why: Melatonin acts at MT1 and MT2 receptors and also at a third site, 'MT3', which turned out to be the enzyme **NRH-quinone oxidoreductase 2** and is probably not involved in sleep physiology.

whyNot: **MAO-B** is the enzyme that metabolizes N-methylhistamine, not caffeine's target.
**H3 blockade** is pitolisant's wake-promoting mechanism, not caffeine's.
Caffeine is an adenosine antagonist; **orexin agonism** is not its mechanism.
**DAT inhibition** is the mechanism proposed for modafinil and armodafinil; caffeine acts indirectly through adenosine receptors.
q10-38.why: Caffeine **blocks adenosine receptors**, easing the fatigue signal of accumulated adenosine and restoring dopamine's affinity at D2 receptors that adenosine had dampened, so dopamine action is enhanced.

whyNot: **Methylphenidate** is approved for narcolepsy, not for shift work disorder or OSA, where use is off-label.
**Pitolisant** is approved for narcolepsy sleepiness, not shift work disorder.
**Sodium oxybate** is approved for cataplexy and sleepiness in narcolepsy, not shift work disorder.
**Caffeine** is a widely used wake promoter but is not described as approved for shift work disorder.
q10-39.why: **Modafinil and armodafinil** are approved for narcolepsy, as OSA adjuncts, and for shift work disorder, an indication amphetamine and methylphenidate do not have.

whyNot: **GABA-B** is the target of sodium oxybate, which promotes sleep rather than wakefulness.
**Melatonin agonists** affect sleep onset and the circadian clock, not daytime wakefulness.
Modafinil is not an **orexin agonist**; any orexin release is a secondary, downstream effect of dopamine.
**H3 blockade** is pitolisant's mechanism; modafinil's histamine release is downstream of dopamine.
q10-40.why: Modafinil primarily inhibits the **dopamine transporter**, raising tonic dopamine; histamine and orexin release follow downstream, so orexin neurons are not required for its wake-promoting effect.

whyNot: **Amphetamine** is a controlled substance with high abuse potential that acts on monoamine transporters, not H3.
**Solriamfetol** is a norepinephrine-dopamine reuptake inhibitor, not an H3 antagonist.
**Armodafinil** is a DAT inhibitor with much reduced abuse potential, not an H3 antagonist.
**Sodium oxybate** acts at GABA-B and GHB receptors and is a tightly regulated controlled substance.
q10-41.why: **Pitolisant** blocks presynaptic H3 autoreceptors, which disinhibits histamine release and promotes wakefulness in narcolepsy; unlike the stimulants and oxybate, it is neither controlled nor known to be abused.

whyNot: **Orexin receptors** are blocked by DORAs for insomnia and are not the sodium oxybate target.
**Benzodiazepine sites on GABA-A** are how benzodiazepines and Z drugs act, not sodium oxybate.
**D2 receptors** matter for dopamine and adenosine coupling in caffeine's action, not oxybate's.
**H1 blockade** is the antihistamine hypnotic route, which oxybate does not use.
q10-42.why: Sodium oxybate (GHB) is a **GABA-B partial agonist** as well as a GHB-receptor agonist; its GABA-B actions are presumed to improve slow-wave sleep and cataplexy.
